back: another name for a Layer 2 broadcast domain. The switch controls which ports belong to which VLAN.
a switch port assigned to a single VLAN. Any device plugged into it is a member of that VLAN.
a port that carries many VLANs and tags each frame with the VLAN it belongs to.
the standard tagging protocol for trunks. The most important field in the tag is the VLAN ID.
the VLAN whose frames cross a trunk untagged. A receiving switch assumes any untagged frame on a trunk belongs to the native VLAN. The default is VLAN 1.
automatically negotiates whether a port becomes an access port or a trunk. Risky, because an attacker can negotiate a trunk.
an attacker who has a trunk tags frames with any VLAN he wants and reaches every VLAN.
routing between VLANs, which always needs a Layer 3 device as the default gateway.
one physical router interface trunked to the switch, with one logical sub-interface per VLAN. Named because the router looks like a lollipop on a stick in the topology.
a logical interface such as Gi0/1.10 that handles frames tagged with one VLAN ID and has its own IP address.
an unused VLAN that unused ports are assigned to and shut down in.
finds parallel Layer 2 paths and blocks all but one so no loop forms.
frames circle endlessly between switches with parallel links. Causes MAC address flapping, excessive forwarding, and possibly denial of service.
the switch keeps relearning the same source MAC on different ports because a looping frame arrives on both.
the message STP uses for negotiation and loop detection.
bridge priority plus base MAC address. The lowest bridge ID wins.
the single switch with the lowest bridge ID. All of its ports forward for the VLAN it is root for.
the port closest to the root bridge by STP path cost, which receives the best BPDU on the switch. Every switch except the root bridge has exactly one.
the port that can send the best BPDU for a particular VLAN on a segment.
a port that doesn't forward packets, to prevent loops. Shown as Altn BLK (alternate, blocking) in the book's output.
Cisco's default, with a separate STP instance for each VLAN. Five VLANs means five instances.
the first 15 seconds on a new port. STP looks for BPDUs and doesn't learn MAC addresses.
the next 15 seconds. STP still looks for BPDUs and also fills the MAC address table.
skips listening and learning and goes straight to forwarding. Only for ports to a single host.
Cisco proprietary 802.1D improvements for faster convergence after a topology change.
newer STP that absorbed many of those Cisco enhancements. Cisco's per-VLAN version is rapid-pvst.
err-disables an access port when a BPDU arrives on it, since users never send legitimate BPDUs.
stops a port from becoming a root port toward a new, remote root switch.
the status of a port shut down by a violation.
limits how many MAC addresses a switch port can learn.
port security learns MAC addresses dynamically and writes them into the running configuration.
the switch's MAC address table.
thousands of frames with bogus source MACs fill the table, so the switch floods all frames to every port in the VLAN and the attacker can sniff them.
many DHCP requests with different source MACs exhaust the DHCP pool. The book uses the name DHCP spoofing for the exhaustion attack and also says DHCP snooping protects against a starvation attack.
an unauthorized server handing out wrong information, such as a false default gateway.
acts like a firewall between untrusted hosts and trusted DHCP servers.
records untrusted hosts and their leased IP addresses. DAI also uses it.
DHCP snooping and DAI forward from trusted ports without checks. All ports are untrusted by default.
a DHCP option the switch inserts, as the snooping output shows. Its name, the relay agent information option, is not in the book.
maps an IP address to a MAC address with a broadcast request inside one broadcast domain.
an ARP reply sent with no request. ARP accepts it, which allows spoofing.

front: ARP spoofing and ARP cache poisoning
back: forged ARP replies bind the victim's IP to the attacker's MAC.
intercepts, logs, and discards ARP packets with invalid IP-to-MAC bindings. Prevents spoofing of Layer 2 information by hosts.
prevents spoofing of Layer 3 (IP) information by hosts on the switch.
authenticates users before letting their frames into the network (covered in Chapter 4).
limits the amount of broadcast or multicast traffic flowing through the switch.
Cisco's Layer 2 discovery protocol from 1994. Devices advertise to a multicast address. Leaks device type, hardware and software versions, and VLAN and IP details.
the IEEE standard discovery protocol. Full name: Station and Media Access Control Connectivity Discovery.
LLDP for Media Endpoint Devices, an extension for voice.
a Layer 2 data plane control listed in Table 6-2. The book doesn't explain it in this chapter.
Cisco framework that breaks the infrastructure into three planes and secures each. A holistic approach, not one feature.
traffic between an administrator and the device itself, such as SSH. A failure can mean losing the ability to manage the device.
protocols devices run on their own, such as routing protocols. A failure can mean the router can't learn or share routes.
transit traffic forwarded through the device between clients and servers.
traffic going through the device. **Nontransit traffic** is traffic going to the device itself.
the router's CPU.
filters and rate-limits traffic destined to the router itself, applied to the logical control plane interface.
finer-grained version of CoPP that splits control plane traffic into three sub-interfaces.
prioritizes critical packets to the route processor, such as routing updates and Layer 2 keepalives. Not strictly a security feature.
reduces the risk of SYN-flood attacks, along with firewall services.
inhibits malicious traffic from entering the network.
the path that sends packets from the forwarding hardware up to the route processor.
packets the CPU must handle, which costs CPU performance.
a CEF entry whose next hop is the device itself, shown as "receive". Covers interface IPs, multicast, and broadcast addresses.
Cisco's forwarding table. CEF exception traffic, such as keepalives and expiring TTLs, must go to the CPU.
drops a packet if its source address wouldn't be reachable out the interface it came in on. The book also calls it unicast reverse path verification and reverse path checks.
management traffic shares the networks (VLANs) used by user traffic. Considered less secure.
a completely separate network, or at least a separate VLAN, used only for management.
local management through a blue rollover cable. By default asks for no username or password.
the lines used by SSH and Telnet sessions.
the auxiliary port.
the CLI an administrator gets after login. Also called character mode.
user accounts in the router's running configuration.
an ordered list of up to four AAA methods, tried left to right. Can be default or custom (named).
applies to the whole device unless a custom list is applied to a line or interface.
must be created, then referenced in line or interface configuration mode. Can be reused on many lines.
tries a long list of words as passwords, one after another.
tries every possible character string up to a set length.
locks a local AAA user account after a configured number of failed logins. Only an administrator can unlock it.
0 to 15. Level 1 is user mode (prompt ends with >). Level 15 is privileged mode, reached with enable.
levels 2 to 14 with commands moved down from level 15. A user gets the commands at his level and below.
a named subset of commands. A user in the view can use only those commands. Many users can share one view.
the default view, entered with enable view and the enable secret, used to create other views.
older Cisco AAA server the book lists as a way to implement RBAC.
approves, communicates, and tracks configuration changes, whatever an administrator's access level.
scrambles plaintext passwords stored in the configuration (type 7). Stops shoulder surfing.
hashed password for privileged mode. Should not match any other password on the device.
encrypted CLI access, replacing plaintext Telnet. Provides confidentiality.
what a server reports when it runs 2.0 but stays backward compatible with older versions (RFC 4253, section 5.1).
plaintext remote CLI. Use it only out of band, inside a VPN, or both.
encrypted GUI management. Use it instead of HTTP.
reads and changes device information. Versions 1 and 2c lack proper encryption and authentication. Version 3 adds both.
SNMP's access control, granting read or read-write access to the whole SNMP tree.
SNMP's hierarchical tree structure. Less intuitive and more prone to security issues than YANG.
an unsolicited message from the device that alerts the management station to an event.
runs over SSH, uses YANG models, encodes configuration data in XML, and supports atomic transactions.
runs over HTTPS, uses YANG models, and supports role-based access control.
NETCONF's fine-grained access control.
a series of configuration changes that is either fully committed or entirely rolled back on error.
formal data modeling language with a standard syntax. Models are modules of statements describing structure, data types, and constraints.
open-source protocol that uses gRPC as transport and YANG models. Supports streaming telemetry and configuration. Increasingly replacing older management protocols.
the message definition syntax used in the book's gNMI example.
plug-ins and tools for learning and testing YANG, NETCONF, RESTCONF, and gNMI.
a management system that can push configurations to devices.
log messages sent in plain text from syslog clients (routers, switches) to syslog servers that receive and store them.
log storage in router memory, rotated first in, first out (FIFO). Lost on reboot.
0 to 7. The higher the level, the more detailed the logs.
relating events across many systems. Needs accurate, synchronized timestamps.
synchronizes device clocks. A Cisco router can be an NTP server for the local network and a client of another server at the same time.
shown in show ntp status. Its meaning, the number of hops from the reference clock, is not in the book.
sends false time from a spoofed source IP. NTP authentication prevents it.

the traditional router operating system. **IOS-XE** is for enterprise routers, **IOS-XR** for service provider routers, and **NX-OS** for data center devices. The book calls them all IOS in this section.
keeps a secure working copy of the IOS image and startup configuration that a remote user can't delete.
the secured image and startup configuration files.
the first step when a router boots, before it looks for an image in flash and loads it into RAM.
where the startup configuration lives. Deleting flash and NVRAM causes long downtime.
128 bits (16 bytes), eight groups of four hex characters separated by colons.
usually the right 64 bits. The network ID is usually the left 64 bits.
replaces one or more consecutive all-zero groups. Usable only once per address.
routable. First group in the range 2000 to 3FFF. Configured manually, learned with a router solicitation, or learned through DHCPv6.
begins with FE80. Used only on the local network. Created automatically if not configured.
the third IPv6 address type the book names. Not explained further.
builds the 64-bit interface ID from the 48-bit MAC by inserting FFFE in the middle and inverting the seventh bit from the left.
::1, which is 127 zeros followed by a 1. IPv4 used the 127 range.
FF02::1, joined by every IPv6 device. FF02 means link-local scope.
FF02::2, joined by routers with IPv6 routing enabled.
FF02::9. RIPv2 in IPv4 uses 224.0.0.9.
FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx, where x is the last 24 bits of the host ID. Joined for every unicast and anycast address, so neighbor solicitations avoid broadcasts.
an address that appears more than once in the network. The network chooses the best one, for example two DNS servers sharing an address.

replaces ARP. Uses ICMPv6 and multicast to discover the network address, routers, and neighbors. The book calls it Network Discovery Protocol in the new risks list but Neighbor Discovery Protocol in Table 6-4. Neighbor Discovery is the correct name.
the ND request and reply.
the router advertisement message routers use to announce themselves, the target of RA Guard. The book never spells out RA. Rogue RAs enable man-in-the-middle attacks.
hosts assign their own IPv6 address. The acronym SLAAC is not in the book.
IPv6 DHCP. Hosts can use it for extra information, such as DNS servers.
IPv6's replacement for IPv4 IP options. Can be misused.
lists intermediate nodes the packet must pass, like IP source routing.
addresses that should never be a valid source or destination.
a device running IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time.
carrying IPv6 packets inside IPv4 across an IPv4-only part of the network.
an automatic tunnel mechanism. Avoid it, because automatic tunnels are dynamic and hard to control.

validates that IPv6 neighbors are legitimate.

builds a trusted binding table from ND messages and drops ND messages that don't conform.
new ND options plus two new messages, CPS (Certification Path Solicitation) and CPA (Certification Path Answer), against ND spoofing and redirection. Platform support is limited.

blocks data traffic from an unknown source, filters on destination, puts all active destinations in the binding table, and blocks traffic to unidentified destinations. Defends against neighbor cache resource starvation.
an attacker spoofs many IPv6 destinations quickly and overwhelms the router's temporary cache entries.
stops a rogue router from injecting routes or learning the routing tables.
sends the password in the clear in every update. Easy to subvert.
sends a hash instead of the password and protects update contents from tampering. Still open to brute-force and dictionary attacks if the password is weak.
global configuration holding numbered keys and key strings. Used by EIGRP and RIPv2, not OSPF.
the only algorithms BGP supports. The book recommends HMAC-SHA1-12.

holds the BGP MD5 digest. Created by RFC 2385, now obsoleted by TCP option Kind 29. Kind 29 is TCP-AO (TCP Authentication Option, RFC 5925); that name and RFC are not in the book but are worth knowing.
keychain authentication between BGP peers, allowing hitless key rollover.
changing keys without dropping the session. Time based, so clock skew affects it.
a configurable margin that extends the accept window before and after rollover.
a control plane protocol the book lists with routing protocols and ICMP.
time synchronization. The book states it twice.
blocked toward the DNS servers in the IPv6 ACL example, and matched as "domain" in the CoPP ACL.
matched as "telnet" in the CoPP ACL. Plaintext. The number is not in the book but is worth knowing.
encrypted CLI and the transport for NETCONF. The number is not in the book but is worth knowing.
secure GUI management and RESTCONF transport. The number is not in the book but is worth knowing.
plaintext web management. Put it in a VPN if it must be used. The number is not in the book but is worth knowing.
what DHCP snooping inspects. The numbers are not in the book but are worth knowing.
the book's example of traffic to block with an ACL if policy forbids it, and the DHCP snooping database is saved to a tftp URL. The number is not in the book but is worth knowing.
